messages.subject_clean: Which analysis could be performed Poppr if I have Genomewide SNP data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> This would be a naive question to ask in this group, but it is important to me.

Naïve questions are quite welcome in this group, as it provides a resource for others who will likely have the same question :)

>
> I am doing a genomewide SNP analysis on a clonal organism and I am using GATK for the same. My output file contains SNPs is in the form of VCF file and I would like to perform various analysis mentioned in the paper. In that case how should I proceed or start with?
>
>

This is a good question. One important factor we left out of the Frontiers paper was how exactly to import genome-wide data from VCF format. There are two packages that you can use to extract genotypes from a VCF file, pegas (https://github.com/emmanuelparadis/pegas) and vcfR (https://github.com/knausb/vcfR).
Both of these packages have valuable tools for analysis and visualization of genomic data. From either of these packages, you can convert to a matrix, which you can then convert to a genlight object (see the adegenet "genomics" tutorial: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/blob/master/tutorials/tutorial-genomics.pdf).

Before you start, I would recommend at this time to install the github versions of the packages as there are many bug fixes and improvements that aren't on CRAN as of yet. You can do this using devtools (you must also have a C compiler working on your computer, see here for links to options https://github.com/grunwaldlab/poppr/#stable-and-development-versions):

if (!require("devtools")) install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("emmanuelparadis/pegas/pegas")
devtools::install_github("knausb/vcfR@devel")
devtools::install_github("thibautjombart/adegenet")
devtools::install_github("grunwaldlab/poppr@devel")

Once you have your data in a genlight object, convert it to a snpclone object with the function as.snpclone() (yes, I know there are quite a few steps to get here). This will make sure that you can have mutlilocus genotype definitions travel with your data. From here, you can:

Calculate raw genetic distance with bitwise.dist()
Define multilocus lineages with mlg.filter()
Calculate sliding windows of the standardized index of association with win.ia()
Randomly sample loci for the standardized index of association with samp.ia()
Construct minimum spanning networks with poppr.msn()
Create boostrapped dendrograms with aboot()

Hope that helps.

Best,

Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The vcfR package is still under development (by me), but I think It might have what you need. There is a read.vcf function to read in vcf files and a vcfR2genind function to make a genind object.

There are a few limitations to working on genomic data in R. The big thing is that memory may be a limiting factor. Because of this I advocate working on a single chromosome (supercontig or contig depending on your genome). And some functions in other packages may not yet scale well to genome size problems. For example,  my vcfR2genind calls adegenet's df2genind, the later of which appears to have problems with large data sets. Although I have not tried the github versions as Zhian has recommended.

Good luck!
Brian

messages.subject_clean: [poppr] aboot on matrix object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Juan,

I apologize, but I believe that is a mistake on my part. The function does not support matrices. I believe I put that in because functions such as nei.dist do support matrices. This will be cleared up in the next version.

Luckily, since each column represents a separate locus, you can perform your bootstrap with the package ape.

There are four steps:

1. create a tree generating function e.g. myTreeFun <- function(x){ nj(nei.dist(x)) } # This will calculate Nei's distance and then create a neighbor-joining tree. You can change the distance or tree function if you wish.
2. calculate the tree for your observed data: myTree <- myTreeFun(myData)
3. use the observed data, tree, and tree function with the ape function "boot.phylo":
    node_labels <- ape::boot.phylo(x = myData, phy = myTree, FUN = myTreeFun, B = 1000)
4. add the node labels to your tree: myTree$node.labels <- node_labels

Hope that helps,
Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For context, this post is a product of the following posts:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/poppr/hgEwoowW3gA

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/poppr/2oLpsGlI54Y

For further information on strata, type help("strata", package = "adegenet") in your R console. Since the strata slot is optional, it is empty by default. It takes a data frame where the rows represent samples and the columns represent the different population strata that each individual could take.

In your example, you only have 1 population stratum which defines 4 populations, thus you would only have 1 column for the strata.

As outlined in section 2.1 of the strata tutorial <https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/blob/master/tutorials/tutorial-strata.pdf>, you can define the strata using the function strata() with a data frame like so:

strata(myData) <- data.frame(Pop = pop(myData)) # create the strata
head(strata(myData))                            # show the results

This will create the data frame with a single column called "Pop" and then show you the top of the resulting data frame. I'm using "Pop" here because it's generic, but you can change it to anything that's meaningful. From here, you can use the poppr.amova() function like so:

poppr.amova(myData, hier = ~Pop)

If you find that you want to do a hierarchical AMOVA and you have definitions for subpopulations, you can add those definitions to your object with the function addStrata().

Hope that helps,

Zhian

Hi Jigar,

I'm afraid your genome size is not very informative as to how large an object your data set will require. The real issue is the number of variants (rows) and the number of samples (columns). I'd suggest you give it a try though. The function read.vcf includes a parameter 'limit' to try and keep you from using all your memory. If you exceed this limit it should give you a message with a guess as to how much memory you might need. You can then try again with a new parameterization for limit.

The number of supercontigs you have is not really so great. I worked through a project this morning with ~5,000 contigs. I use something like:

Files <- list.files("./directory_with_vcfs/", pattern="vcf$", full.names=TRUE)
for(i in 1:length(Files)){
  x <- read.vcf(Files[i])
  # some sort of processing of each vcf
}

To cycle through large numbers of files.

Also, vcfR2genind does not appear to be working well for large objects. I believe this has to do with an adegenet function. I have yet to try the version on github though. The function vcfR2genlight may be a better option.

Good luck!
Brian

Hi Alex,

>From what you've provided, I can surmise that "d" is a genind or genclone object containing data for individuals (you would get a completely different error, otherwise). The code you've provided me looks like you are trying to convert whatever is in the "other" slot into a data frame and use that for the strata (this would only work if all elements in the "other" slot are the same size as your data).

You can get the same error with the following code:

library(adegenet)
data(nancycats)
strata(nancycats) <- data.frame(other(nancycats))

## Error: Number of rows in data frame not equal to number of individuals in object.

You can see why this failed if you looked at the number of rows in the data frame you're using to define your strata:

nrow(data.frame(other(nancycats)))

## [1] 17

nInd(nancycats)

## [1] 237

It's possible that you don't have anything in the "other" slot, which would give you the same error.

I've written a small tutorial about dealing with strata here: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/blob/master/tutorials/tutorial-strata.pdf
You have two options to use strata (detailed in the tutorial):

1. Import a data frame of strata defined for each sample from a separate file with read.table() and then use strata() as you did above.
2. Define your strata in the population column in your import file and then use splitStrata() to split up the different strata into columns.

After that, you can use genind2genpop to convert to a genpop object using any definition of strata and then use aboot to bootstrap.

I hope that helps. Let me know if you have any further questions.

Zhian

messages.subject_clean: Technical Question about Calculated G value
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The poppr() command does NOT automatically scale G with a rarefaction to the minimum sample size. You can perform this using the diversity_ci() or diversity_boot() functions with the option rarefy = TRUE. An example is laid out in the multilocus genotype vignette: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/poppr/vignettes/mlg.html#jack-knife-rarefaction

Here's some sample code to extract the rarefied estimate of G with a confidence interval:

library('poppr')
data(monpop)
splitStrata(monpop) <- ~Tree/Year/Symptom
setPop(monpop) <- ~Symptom/Year
mondiv <- diversity_ci(monpop, n = 1000L, rarefy = TRUE, raw = FALSE)

## Samples for rarefaction: 19
mondiv[, c("G.est", "G.ci")]
##       G.est            G.ci
## BB_9  13.88     (8.805, 19)
## FR_9   8.43 (5.232, 12.448)
## BB_10 19.00            <NA>
## FR_10 13.89     (9.256, 19)
## BB_11 19.00            <NA>
## FR_11  8.25  (4.454, 13.37)
## Total 15.52    (10.939, 19)

Hope that helps!

Zhian

Hello Jennifer,

Thank you for giving a detailed description of your error and examples of data to produce the error.

I believe this is an error that originated in the "adegenet" package, specifically with the function "df2genind". Basically, your sample names were being interpreted as numbers instead of names.This issue was fixed some time ago on the development version of adegenet <https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet>.

Both adegenet and poppr are actually set to have new versions released soon. You can see what's modified in poppr here <https://github.com/grunwaldlab/poppr/blob/master/NEWS> and see what's modified in adegenet here <https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/blob/master/ChangeLog>.

You can install the development versions of adegenet and poppr using the package "devtools". Since you're on a Windows system, be sure to install Rtools <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/> first.

devtools::install_github(c("thibautjombart/adegenet", "grunwaldlab/poppr"))

Best,
Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jessica,

You threw a real curveball on that one. The problem here lies in some of the allele calls for your Rosie1 locus. You have some alleles denoted as "18.5".

The reason why this doesn't work is because adegenet is not expecting alleles to be fractional. The genind object is constructed such that each column represents an allele and is denoted as [Locus].[Allele]. This convention is used so the program can easily work with alleles and loci in a predictable fashion. When you have a column called "Rosie1.18.5", it becomes unclear whether the locus is called "Rosie1.18" or if the allele is "18.5".

My suggested solution: Multiply all of those values by 2 before they come into R, so you will get integers.

If you wanted to use these values for Bruvo's distance:

1. Half-steps violate the assumptions of the model for stepwise mutation.
2. All values are rounded to integers before calculation, thus the value of 18.5 will become 18 (R rounds using the IEC 60559 standard, which is "go to the even digit").

Hope that helps. Let me know if you have any other questions.

Zhian

> The reason why this doesn't work is because adegenet is not expecting alleles to be fractional. The genind object is constructed such that each column represents an allele and is denoted as [Locus].[Allele]. This convention is used so the program can easily work with alleles and loci in a predictable fashion. When you have a column called "Rosie1.18.5", it becomes unclear whether the locus is called "Rosie1.18" or if the allele is "18.5".
>
> My suggested solution: Multiply all of those values by 2 before they come into R, so you will get integers.
>
> If you wanted to use these values for Bruvo's distance:
>
> 1. Half-steps violate the assumptions of the model for stepwise mutation.
> 2. All values are rounded to integers before calculation, thus the value of 18.5 will become 18 (R rounds using the IEC 60559 standard, which is "go to the even digit").
>
> Hope that helps. Let me know if you have any other questions.
